body: A man is walking home in the dark with a small radio in his shirt pocket, turning the dial with his thumb the way he has since he was a boy. There is a football commentary. There is a phone-in about the price of fuel. There is a station playing love songs in a language he can follow but does not think in, and near the top of the band a preacher, translated, running half a second behind himself. He turns that one past as well. By the time he reaches his gate he has been all the way up the band and back down it, and he has not heard anybody sing to God in the language his mother scolded him in.

There is nothing unusual about that walk. It is the ordinary radio experience of a very large share of the people alive, and the reason for it has never been that nobody wanted to build him a station. It is that until quite recently nobody could afford to.

Consider what it used to take to put one round-the-clock worship station on air in, say, Amharic. A catalogue of music in that language. Presenters who speak it. A studio, and the hours to fill it. Artwork. Somebody to schedule it. Licensing for every song played. And then a transmitter, or a bandwidth bill for a stream nobody is paying to hear.

It is worth being precise about what kind of cost that is, because the word makes it sound like a price somebody could raise once. It is not. Every item on that list is a job, and most of them are jobs that recur tomorrow — the schedule has to be filled again, the presenter has to come in again, the licence falls due again. Worse, all of it has to exist before the first listener does. Nobody tunes to a frequency that is playing nothing, so the whole apparatus must be paid for in full during the months when the audience is zero, by people who cannot yet be shown that anybody wants it. That is the barrier. It was never conviction.
This band opened with 40 international frequencies carrying 29 languages besides English. The smallest of them, Bulgarian, went on air with twelve songs.

That last figure is the commitment, and it is the sort of decision a broadcaster with a budget cannot make. A permanent frequency was assigned to a language with twelve songs to its name, and it cannot be taken back later and handed to a station somebody would actually pay for. It will sound thin for a while and it was opened anyway, because the alternative is to hold the number in reserve until the language earns it, and languages have been waiting to earn it for a hundred years. The gospel was never the thing in short supply. The transmitters were.

What that scarcity produced is a map that ought to be more scandalous than it is. Christian broadcasting has always followed advertising revenue and donor bases, which means it follows wealth, which means a comfortable city can carry a dozen stations competing over the same listeners while a language with tens of millions of speakers has almost nothing. Nobody planned that. It is simply what happens when the cost of a transmitter is allowed to decide who gets sung to.

Most of that stack has now collapsed, item by item. The music can be written in the language rather than translated into it. The presenter can be a persona who actually speaks it. Artwork is minutes rather than a commission. Licensing does not apply at all, because the catalogue is owned outright rather than rented. What is left is bandwidth and machines, which is why the multilanguage section could open all at once instead of adding one language a year as donations allowed.
The work did not get easier. The barrier keeping most of the world out simply turned out to have been a money barrier almost the whole way down.

It is worth being fair to what came before, because the old answer to this problem was not laziness. It was translation, and it did enormous good. Ministries dubbed one English service into forty languages, put it on shortwave, and people heard the gospel who would not otherwise have heard it — some of them behind borders no missionary could cross, and some of them are still alive. But a translated broadcast is a guest in the language it arrives in. The stresses land in the wrong places, the idioms come out slightly formal, the hymn tune argues with the shape of the words, and the presenter is audibly reading. It works. Everybody listening can also tell it is an import.
A translated hymn is a visitor in a language. A written one lives there.

A woman of seventy-one is minding her granddaughter on a Thursday afternoon in a flat four thousand miles from where she was born. The child is six, speaks the language of the country she was born in, and understands her grandmother’s the way you understand weather. The old woman puts a station on because the flat is too quiet with only the two of them in it. A song comes on that she does not know — it is new, it is not from her church, and the arrangement is not what she would have chosen — but every word in it is hers. Some hours later the child sings four of them back at her, in the wrong order, while looking for her shoes.
Nothing in that afternoon was translated and nothing in it was explained. A language a child hears sung is a language the child keeps a piece of, and no amount of dubbing has ever managed that.

The honest cost is that these stations are new and they sound new. A catalogue of twelve songs repeats, and you will notice by the second afternoon. Several of the language editions carry two dozen tracks and no more. Anybody who grew up with a well-funded commercial station in a major language will find these thin, and they are thin, and saying otherwise would be a small lie told for a good cause.

But thin is what a beginning sounds like, and the comparison that matters is not with a rich station. It is with silence, which is what was there before. Every unremarkable, well-stocked station in a major language began at exactly this point, with somebody deciding the language was worth a permanent number before there was much to put on it. The repetition is not a defect in the plan. It is the sound of a catalogue that has started.

So the collapse of that cost stack is not a technical footnote and it is not a boast about tools. It is the reason a language can now be given a frequency on the grounds that people speak it, rather than on the grounds that enough of them can be sold something. The transmitter used to decide, and the transmitter was never a spiritual instrument. It was a bill.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 assigned frequencies, 46 of them live at this moment. 40 of those numbers belong to the international band and carry 29 languages besides English — Spanish and Portuguese and Mandarin and Hindi and Arabic, and also Bulgarian and Thai and Czech and Hungarian, which is to say the languages that would never have made anybody a business case. Each is hosted in its own language rather than translated into it. They sit together in one stretch of the dial, so a listener can walk the nations the way you would walk a band.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 327.20 — Bulgaria Inspire. It is the newest and smallest catalogue here, opened at the twelve-song threshold so that the language would have a frequency to grow into, and it is therefore the clearest demonstration of everything above. Leave it on and the rotation will come round in front of you. That is the point rather than the problem: you are listening to the first weeks of something that, on the old arithmetic, would simply never have happened at all. And if one of the 29 on this band is yours, or your mother’s, go there instead — that is the frequency this article is actually about.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, because that is the hardware most of the world is holding. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which languages people are actually reaching for, which is how the next one gets opened.

So take this as an invitation rather than an appeal. Put HM 327.20 on for twenty minutes this evening while you are cooking, and listen to how few songs there are. Then consider that the same thing is true, right now, in 29 languages at once, and that not one of them was waiting on somebody’s conviction. They were waiting on a transmitter, and the transmitter has stopped being the thing that decides.
